A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCBL mechanism-design work. The main texts, algorithms, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching content across renaming and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical results, proofs, and symbolic examples throughout the main text and Appendices A–D, without original empirical or numerical evaluation results.

after.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix C report original computational results for a three-agent allocation example. Appendix C explicitly attributes the numerical optimization outcomes to computations performed in Mathematica.

M1.justification: MCBL retains its collection-adjustment loops, leverage condition, corruption rule, estimators, and recommended truthful strategies. Compute-Bargaining-Approx is renamed Compute-n-Approx, while the existing ability to accept alternative bargaining allocations is retained.

E1.justification: The Gaussian mean-estimation task and heterogeneous-cost setting remain unchanged. The new numerical illustration instantiates the one-dimensional setting already discussed in v1 Section 3; its agent count and cost parameters do not introduce different task requirements or data distributions.

E2.justification: Neither version reports numerical comparisons of competing mechanisms against MCBL. The new Figure 1 compares compliant work allocations within the sample-mean mechanism; Chen et al.'s mechanism remains a theoretical reference rather than an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces a numerical evaluation procedure comparing five allocation choices with three agents, one distribution, sigma = 10, and costs 0.033, 0.066, and 0.1. v1 contains no corresponding numerical protocol.

E4.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix C add a computed case study examining how IR constraints and Nash or egalitarian objectives redistribute collection burdens and benefits. v1 discusses these fairness issues symbolically without this comparative numerical analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, experimental seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Randomized strategies and Gaussian variances are mathematical model components retained across versions.

E6.justification: Appendix C adds allocation and penalty values absent from v1. For example, the IR-constrained optimum collects (71, 7, 0) points with reported penalties approximately (3.63, 1.72, 1.28); egalitarian bargaining collects (41, 21, 14), with penalties approximately 2.69 each.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorems 2–3 and proofs concerning always-IR and dominant-strategy guarantees, revises the unfavorable-case efficiency derivation, and supplies additional proofs of retained auxiliary results. The original hardness theorem survives as Theorem 4. Theorem 5's per-agent factor-eight guarantee already appeared in v1 Remark 1 and is not wholly new.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary expand from one hardness result to three, adding impossibility claims concerning dominant strategies and IR regardless of other agents' behavior. The existing approximation and truthful-contribution claims remain, while fairness becomes a separately emphasized contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new stronger-guarantee bounds as preventing collaboration benefits that improve with agent count and develops the IR-versus-fairness tradeoff through the numerical example. It removes v1's concluding limitation about worst-case-only optimality and the open question of cost-adaptive hardness.

D1.justification: Appendix C identifies Mathematica as the computational tool and provides the optimization objectives and parameters underlying Figure 1. This adds concrete reproducibility information for computations absent from v1.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around truthful collaboration, cooperative valuation, and monetary data collection. New references include Capitaine et al., Chen–Shen–Zheng, Ghosh et al., and Hardt et al.; much generic mechanism-design background is removed. v2 also explicitly claims novelty for combining cooperative work allocation with noncooperative enforcement.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and problem exposition are extensively rewritten. Fairness moves into a dedicated Section 6, baseline derivations and the corruption-coefficient definition move to appendices, and the proofs are reorganized from Appendices A–D into A–I.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout with running headers. v2 adds the five-panel Figure 1 with workload and penalty axes, and relocates and reformats the algorithm displays.

improvement.justification: Clearer organization and the explicit fairness computations improve accessibility. However, new Theorem 2 covers all admitted costs, while Fact 1 and Appendix F.3 allow every agent's standalone penalty to be infinite. In those cases always-IR is automatic, yet truthful sharing can yield finite penalties, contradicting the theorem's lower bound. This affects a new headline contribution, leaving the net quality effect uncertain despite the presentation gains.
